source.title: Shadow Unlearning: A Neuro-Semantic Approach to Fidelity-Preserving Faceless Forgetting in LLMs
source.authors: Dinesh P. Srivasthav; Ashok Urlana; Rahul Mishra; B. Garlapati; P. Kumaraguru

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table content is flattened, making individual Table 18 values difficult to assign reliably to models and attack conditions.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether prompting attacks weaken unlearning, using NSPU and its own evaluation metrics rather than the original studies' unlearning and recovery procedures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports three prompting attacks against NSPU: paraphrasing, adding relevant context, and appending answer tokens. It states that the attacked models' retention–forgetting tradeoff outperformed baseline methods. Table 18 contains separate attack and model results, but its flattened layout does not allow reliable assignment of all numerical values. The paper also reports unrelated main-method comparisons and activation analyses; these do not test fine-tuning recovery, quantization recovery, or restoration by ablation.
record.test_reason: In an appendix, the paper tests its own new unlearning method (NSPU, on anonymized PII data) against three prompting attacks. This bears on version F, a newer method claimed to resist attacks. The only measure is a composite retention–forgetting tradeoff, so it cannot isolate whether prompting recovered forgotten facts (version E).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that NSPU enables unlearning from anonymized forget sets with better retention–forgetting tradeoffs, privacy (membership-inference/SQS) and efficiency than the baselines. The robustness claim is secondary, in an appendix: attacked NSPU still beats the baselines on the tradeoff.
record.recipe_differences: NSPU is a new projection-based unlearning method, evaluated with paraphrase, additional-context, and hard-tokens attacks. It is not a reproduction of the cited unlearning methods or their recovery tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The tested prompt attack type varies: paraphrase, additional context, and hard tokens. The paper also reports that results vary across models and data variants, but the attack-specific numerical mapping is unclear in the flattened table.
record.code_released: The paper says code is available at Github, but provides no URL in the text.
record.problems: Attack results are summarized using tradeoff metrics rather than a direct measure of recovered targeted knowledge. The flattened Table 18 prevents reliable assignment of its individual attack results to model-condition pairs. No uncertainty estimates are stated for these results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 18 reports separate metric values for methods, models, and attack variants, but the flattened extraction does not reliably preserve their assignments. These numerical entries were left out rather than guessed; see Appendix P, Table 18.

untested.parts: No accuracy-to-chance measure on targeted knowledge; NSPU is a new method, not the originals' methods.
No ablation recovery. The filter is a final-layer projection that leaves earlier layers intact, but the paper only argues earlier layers hold no PII; it does not test this.
Paraphrase, context and answer-prefix attacks are run, but only a composite tradeoff is reported, so recovery of forgotten facts is not measured. Jailbreaks and other languages are not tried.
Robustness is not tested against fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or white-box probing of early layers; the authors concede the last point in their limitations.

missing.what: Per-model Table 18 component values for the attacked variants (NSPU-P/A/H), especially forget-side terms such as forget gain, forget instability and forget ratio, which bear directly on recovery. The flattened layout makes the model assignment uncertain.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's E 'challenges' label is unjustified: no measure of recovered knowledge exists, so no verdict on E. Unlearned outputs often fabricate plausible values (Table 16), and the authors count this as success. The record's claim that Table 18 values can't be assigned is overstated: the aggregate columns are identifiable, though the model ordering is uncertain.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether targeted knowledge is brought near chance and whether simple attacks fail under that condition.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack.
No direction-ablation recovery test or analysis demonstrating that the tested unlearning merely blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests paraphrasing, added relevant context, and answer-token-prefix attacks; does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context provision of forgotten information.
Tests NSPU against the three prompting attacks described in the paper, not against fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization attacks.

rows.subject: NSPU attacked variant
rows.operation_detail: Paraphrase attack: evaluate unlearning with paraphrased versions of original questions.
rows.measure: Retention–forgetting tradeoff, reported using HPS, CES, HRS, HCNLL, and their aggregate.
rows.baseline: Baseline methods GA, GD, KLM, DPO, and NPO are shown in Table 18; individual attack-to-model numerical assignments are not reliably recoverable from the flattened text.
rows.value: The authors state that attacked models' retention–forgetting tradeoff outperformed baseline methods.
rows.note: The paper describes NSPU as resilient to paraphrasing, but the stated comparison with baselines does not establish that the attack recovered no knowledge.
rows.check: Table 18 is readable enough to give aggregates. I read the four columns ending in NSPU 4.073, 7.849, 8.669 and 4.882 as the aggregate scores; model mapping is uncertain. Under paraphrase (NSPU-P) these become 4.431, 5.344, 6.841 and 4.482. That is a drop of about 20–30% in two models, still above every baseline. The composite mixes retain and forget terms, so it cannot show knowledge recovery; unlink from E.

relation.reason: Appendix P attacks NSPU and compares the attacked variants with the baselines, which bears on F. The only measure is a composite score.

tranche.reason: The paper tests its own new method, on anonymized fictitious PII data, against three prompt attacks. That is a new setting with a result on version F. The reader's T2 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: Table 18 is flattened. The label order (Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B, OLMoE, Llama-13B) plus Q.1 (OLMoE has the best Table 1 aggregate, 8.669) suggests the columns are 4.073 LLaMA-7B, 7.849 Mistral-7B, 8.669 OLMoE, 4.882 LLaMA-13B. That is not certain. Robustness is a short appendix result on a composite score only. The pack flags a shared author with an original, so this is not an independent test.

statements.correction: NSPU (Appendix P, Table 18): paraphrase, added-context (60 DI QA pairs) and hard-token prompt attacks on LLaMA-7B, Mistral-7B-instruct, OLMoE-1B-7B-0924 and LLaMA-2-13B. No jailbreak, no optimized prompts, no retrained reference. Attacked aggregates (HPS+CES+HRS+HCNLL) beat GA, GD, KLM, DPO and NPO in all four model columns. Against unattacked NSPU they fall 21-32% in two columns (7.849 to 5.344-5.710; 8.669 to 6.315-6.841) and 8% under paraphrase in a third (4.882 to 4.482). The other cells rise. There is no direct forget-recovery measure.
statements.problem: Every number in it belongs to other studies (Eraser, DUET, Nullify, AdaPop). It cites R1-R3 but says nothing specific about NSPU. NSPU was attacked by paraphrase, added context and hard tokens, not jailbreak or optimized prompts, and has no retrained reference. Its models (LLaMA-7B, Mistral-7B-instruct, OLMoE-1B-7B, LLaMA-2-13B) are outside the stated '3B-8B Llama models'. 'Reduces without removing' fits only loosely, on a composite score.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: NSPU under paraphrase, additional-context, and hard-tokens attacks
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that NSPU remained resilient under these prompt attacks and that attacked models' tradeoff outperformed baselines; the reported evidence is not a direct measure of whether recovery was absent (R1, R2, R3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: NSPU under the three prompting attacks tested
reader_labels.reason: The authors present NSPU as a robust counter-method and report that its attacked variants outperformed baseline methods on the tradeoff evaluation (R1, R2, R3).
